Haven
HAY-vn
noun
From the Saxon haefen, a harbour, akin to have and hold — a place that holds; hence a sheltered anchorage where a ship rides safe out of the reach of the sea.

Biblical Definition

A haven is a harbour — the sheltered water where a vessel lies at rest, held safe from the sea that has been beating her. The word is a place of arrival, and Scripture makes it a place of doctrine. Zebulun’s inheritance is described by it: “Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships” (Gen 49:13). But the great haven of the AV is the last line of the seafarer’s psalm. The Psalmist has taken us out with the merchants: “they that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23); he has raised the stormy wind that lifts up the waves and reeled them to and fro like a drunken man till they are at their wits’ end; he has heard them cry unto the LORD in their trouble; and then, “he maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still” (Psa 107:29). And then the line that ends the voyage: “then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven” (Psa 107:30). Mark that the calm is not the haven. The calm is a mercy granted on the passage; the haven is the end of the passage. The believer’s desired haven is glory — the harbour where the voyage is over, the ship is moored, and there is no more sea.

Webster 1828 Definition

A harbour or port; a sheltered anchorage where ships ride safe; hence a place of rest and refuge.

expand to see more

HAVEN, a harbor; a port; a bay or inlet where ships can ride secure from storms.

From the Saxon haefen, akin to have and hold — a place that holds.

By extension, any shelter, asylum, or place of safety and rest.

Zebulun’s border is described as the haven of the sea and a haven of ships (Gen 49:13).

Psa 107:30 makes the desired haven the end of the storm-tossed voyage.

Key Scripture

Psa 107:30 — "Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven."

Psa 107:23 — "They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;"

Psa 107:29 — "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still."

Gen 49:13 — "Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships; and his border shall be unto Zidon."

Modern Corruption

The corruption is not of the word but of its address: our age seeks the desired haven on this side of the grave and calls every calm an arrival.

expand to see more

Men will have a haven; the only question is where they look for it. The age offers several, all of them anchorages in open water: the retirement that will finally settle everything, the house that will make a family whole, the salary at which anxiety stops, the relationship that ends loneliness, the therapy that closes the old wound for good. Each is offered as harbour and each is a roadstead — sheltered enough to feel like arrival, open enough that the next gale finds you there. Scripture is not cruel about this; the Psalm grants real calms. He does make the storm a calm, and the waves are genuinely still, and the men are genuinely glad. But the psalm does not stop there, and neither should we. A calm is a mercy in the passage. It is not the port.

The desired haven is glorification. Every voyage in this life ends short of it: the believer is brought through storm after storm, quieted, blown out again, quieted again, and every deliverance is a foretaste and none of them is the harbour. The harbour is the LORD Himself, entered at the end — where the sea that has tossed the church since Eden is gone, where John saw the new heaven and the new earth and recorded that there was no more sea. This is why the Christian can lose the calm and keep his gladness. His hope is an anchor of the soul, sure and stedfast, already cast within the veil where his Forerunner is entered; the mooring is fast in the haven before the ship is. He is not sailing hopefully toward a port that may not be there. He is being brought to a haven already prepared, by a Pilot who has never lost a vessel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a harbour — the sheltered water that holds a ship safe at the end of her voyage.

expand to see more

Haven — Saxon haefen, a harbour, akin to have and hold.

The root idea is a place that holds — shelter that keeps what enters it.

By extension it means any refuge, asylum, or place of rest.

Gen 49:13 uses it geographically of Zebulun’s coastal inheritance.

Psa 107:30 uses it doctrinally: the desired haven at the voyage’s end.

Usage

"So he bringeth them unto their desired haven — the end of the voyage, not a lull in it."

"He maketh the storm a calm: the calm is a mercy on the passage, the haven is the port."

"The believer’s haven is glory, where the sea that tossed the church is no more."
